context: The sorted array is nums = [1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 12, 15], with indices starting at 0. The search target is 6 (target = 6). Five consecutive 6s occupy indices 2 through 6. The insertion rule places a new 6 to the left of all existing 6s.
description: The diagram illustrates an initial approach in two steps. In step 1, “Use binary search to find any 6,” ordinary binary search finds the orange cell at index 4, marked by pointer k. This match alone does not tell us how many more 6s lie to its left.

In step 2, “Then scan left to find the leftmost 6,” follow the two curved blue arrows below the array, moving left one cell at a time from k = 4. Pass the 6 at index 3 and reach the blue-highlighted 6 at index 2. The next element to the left, at index 1, is 3, which is less than 6. Index 2 therefore holds the leftmost 6 and is the desired insertion point.

frames.explanation: When there are many duplicates, scanning left can take O(n) time, degrading the overall worst-case complexity. A modified binary search can maintain O(log n) time.
frames.title: Scanning left after a binary search finds a match

summary: Use ordinary binary search to find one occurrence of the target, then scan left to find its leftmost position.
title: Scanning left after a binary search finds a match
